figuresReviewed: Figure 2, p. 4: recursive conditional diffusion world model
tablesReviewed: Table II, p. 5: four vision-based simulation tasks
Table III, p. 6: vision-based Push-T score and timing

synopsis: Generative Predictive Control (GPC) improves a frozen diffusion policy by predicting the consequences of its action proposals, then selecting or refining them before execution. Its separate world model learns from demonstrations plus random exploration. Simulation and small real-world studies support this combination, while rollout cost and incomplete evaluation details limit the strength of broader deployment claims (e02, e03, e10, e12, e16, e18).

problem.text: Behavior cloning can compound errors after drifting away from demonstrated behavior. GPC asks whether learned predictive foresight can correct deployment decisions without retraining the policy. It assumes an action-conditioned dynamics model and an outcome reward or candidate-selection rule are available.

contributions.text: The framework combines proposal ranking, gradient refinement, and their composition around independently learned policy and world-model modules.
A recursive image-space diffusion world model supports direct evaluation of imagined outcomes; zeroing its initial noise at inference is proposed to stabilize action optimization.

inputs: History of low-dimensional states or visual observations, denoted I_t
Candidate action chunks from the pretrained diffusion policy; a learned numerical reward or task-conditioned VLM selector
outputs: A selected or refined robot action chunk for receding-horizon execution
Predicted future states or images used internally for planning

steps.name: Propose from an expert prior
steps.detail: The stochastic diffusion policy maps observation history to plausible action chunks. Its parameters stay frozen during deployment; optimization changes the proposed actions.

steps.name: Predict candidate consequences
steps.detail: State-based dynamics use MLPs. Visual dynamics recursively predict the next image from observation history and the current action, feeding predictions into subsequent steps.

steps.name: Score and choose
steps.detail: GPC-RANK chooses the highest predicted reward among K proposals. GPC-OPT warm-starts from one proposal and performs M gradient-ascent steps through the reward and world model. Their combination optimizes multiple initializations before selection.

training.text: Expert demonstrations are segmented with sliding windows. The policy uses DDPM, a UNet, and a ResNet18 visual encoder; training lasts 300 epochs with AdamW, learning rate 10^-4 and weight decay 10^-6. Images are resized to height 96.

Only the world-model dataset adds random perturbations to expert trajectories. Visual training first supervises one-step prediction, then jointly supervises recursively predicted sequences. The model uses EDM, observation horizon H=4 and three denoising steps.

A ResNet18+MLP predicts numerical rewards from images. Real Push-T reward labels use AprilTag-derived registration losses; cloth labels use normalized progress through successful grasp-and-move operations. State information used to label rewards is distinct from the visual-only real-world inference inputs.

inference.text: The policy uses 100 denoising steps, reported observation horizon H=2, prediction horizon T=16 and action horizon 9. Control replans after executing an action segment. The paper's inclusive indexing is inconsistent with its horizon prose, so exact tensor lengths remain unresolved.

The world model initializes diffusion noise to zero at inference. A differentiable reward enables OPT; RANK can instead query a VLM once per decision using each candidate's final predicted frame and a task prompt, with temperature 0.2. The reported VLM setting uses 10 candidates versus 100 for learned-reward comparisons.

equations.explanation: Equation (2): I_t is the available history, a^(k) a policy proposal, W the world model, R the outcome reward, K the proposal count, and pi the resulting online policy. Selection evaluates predicted consequences.

Equation (4): the initial action chunk is sampled from the policy; ell indexes refinement steps and eta^(ell)>0 is their step size. After M steps the refined chunk is returned. The plus sign implements reward ascent.

Equations (6–7): o denotes images; f_vision is a single-step conditional diffusion predictor. Its denoiser D_phi, with weights phi, decreases noise index tau from N_d to 1. The final image is o^0; repeated physical prediction builds a rollout.

results.setting: Simulation; mean over 100 evaluation seeds, Table I.
results.comparison: Behavior cloning: 0.812; planning with a ground-truth simulator: 0.952.
results.interpretation: The best listed learned-model variant approaches the simulator reference; this state-input result is separate from vision-based evaluation.

results.setting: Table II; 50 evaluation seeds. Authors report common training data, the same pretrained diffusion policy and 100 candidates for enhancement baselines; VLM uses 10.
results.metric: Reported task scores; non-Push-T score definitions are not supplied explicitly
results.value: GPC-RANK: Push-T 0.739; Triangle Drawing 0.767; Block Stacking 0.989; Cube & Sphere Swapping 0.730.
results.comparison: Diffusion Policy: 0.642, 0.724, 0.912, 0.680. VLM variants: Triangle 0.761, Stacking 0.973.
results.interpretation: Learned-reward GPC leads every row. VLM numbers use a different candidate budget; scores should not be averaged across tasks or relabeled success probabilities.

results.setting: Table III; simulation IoU over 100 evaluation seeds; wall-clock seconds per decision.
results.interpretation: Combined planning gains 0.240 absolute IoU over BC at substantial cost. The table labels BC as K=1,M=1, conflicting with the no-refinement baseline elsewhere.

results.setting: Vision-based Push-T, Figure 5; world models trained with versus without exploration.
results.value: Adding exploration improves both RANK and OPT; no exact bar labels are supplied.
results.comparison: Expert-only world-model training gives lower bars for both planners.
results.interpretation: The trend supports broader dynamics coverage, but the comparison adds data and does not isolate exploration diversity from dataset size.

results.setting: Figure 8 and Section V-C; 10 trials for each reported evaluation.
results.metric: Success rate read from plotted bars
results.value: Push-T RANK and OPT: 0.7 each; clothes-folding RANK: 0.7.
results.interpretation: These are executed-task outcomes, unlike imagined-image quality. Small trial counts, absent intervals and unspecified success thresholds limit precision.

limitations.text: The authors identify inference cost as the main limitation: world-model rollouts consume approximately 90–95% of runtime. Their approximately 3-second real-world RANK cycle is a different setting from Table III's simulation timings.

High SSIM and plausible predicted interactions do not establish accurate reward gradients or reliable recovery outside the tested tasks. Zero noise makes predictions deterministic; it does not by itself prove the authors' 'most likely future' interpretation.
Reporting conflicts remain: Table III gives BC M=1 while Table I gives M=0; Figure 6 gives OPT K=0 while Algorithm 1 requires a policy warm start with K=1. Horizon indexing also needs clarification.

reproduction.text: Appendix A lists simulation expert/perturbation counts: Push-T 500/3000 plus seven long-horizon demonstrations; Triangle Drawing 30/100; Block Stacking 50/100; Cube & Sphere 100/100. Real tasks use 100 expert demonstrations per task and five random-play videos, each several minutes.

The supplied methods do not specify exact data splits, world-model phase durations, optimization step-size schedules, action constraints, GPU hardware or software versions. Task success thresholds and several score definitions are also absent. These gaps prevent exact reconstruction from this PDF alone.

Proposed checks should hold the policy fixed and test exploration at matched data volume, then compare zero, fixed-random and resampled world-model noise under matched planning budgets. Measure executed IoU and prediction–outcome agreement, not only predicted reward.

reasoning.text: Separate policy and predictive world-model networks support Dual-system. The world model conditions on proposed actions; it neither jointly emits future observations and executable actions nor infers actions from a desired future. Other mechanisms and Outside quadrants fit this inference-time planning design. The post-training category describes when enhancement occurs, not policy fine-tuning or demonstrated online RL.

discussionQuestions: At matched wall-clock budgets, when does gradient refinement outperform ranking alone?
Does exploration improve corrective dynamics because of its distribution, its volume, or both?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block, left-margin arXiv stamp and author/publication footnote
evidence.detail: Exact title and authors Han Qi, Haocheng Yin, Aris Zhu, Yilun Du, Heng Yang; arXiv:2502.00622v4, 11 March 2026. Accepted RA-L preprint; revised 31 January and accepted 28 February 2026. Harvard University and Georgia Institute of Technology affiliations are listed.

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, Abstract and Section I, motivating question and Contribution
evidence.detail: GPC adds predictive online planning to pretrained frozen diffusion policies to address behavior-cloning deployment errors without policy retraining.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Figure 1(a–b), caption, Algorithm 1 lines 1–10 and instantiation comment; Section II modular-design paragraph
evidence.detail: Policy and world model are independently trained. K proposals may receive M action-gradient updates before ranking. The comment defines RANK by M=0 and OPT by K=1,M>0. Figure 1 stars the highest illustrated reward and shows gradients returning toward the action proposal.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III, Generative policy training, including implementation paragraph
evidence.detail: Sliding-window demonstrations train a DDPM policy with UNet and ResNet18 vision encoder. Reported H=2,T=16, action horizon 9, image height 96, 300 epochs, AdamW learning rate 10^-4, weight decay 10^-6 and 100 inference denoising steps; receding-horizon control.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III, Predictive world modeling
evidence.detail: World-model training combines expert trajectories with human/controller random perturbations that need not solve the task, motivated by broader dynamics excitation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III, Online planning, Equations (1–5); PDF p. 4, opening GPC-RANK+OPT paragraph
evidence.detail: K sampled action chunks are scored through R(W). OPT maximizes predicted reward by positive-step gradient ascent from a policy sample for M iterations. Ranking supports nondifferentiable rewards; the combined method refines multiple initializations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Figure 2 and caption; Section IV, Equations (6–7)
evidence.detail: Visual dynamics recursively apply an action-conditioned one-step image predictor. Observation history enters CONV IN, action enters UNet, and denoising maps noise index tau to tau-1. MLP dynamics are available for low-dimensional states.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section IV, Two-phase training and Remark 1 (Freeze the Noise)
evidence.detail: One-step supervision precedes recursive multistep supervision. H=4 and N_d=3 with EDM. Initial image noise is fixed to zero at inference; authors state stochastic gradients otherwise destabilize OPT and call the deterministic output the most likely prediction, without a formal mode argument.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section V-A; PDF p. 5, Table I and Section V-A continuation
evidence.detail: State Push-T uses simulator states, MLP dynamics and an object-vertex registration loss. Table I averages IoU over 100 seeds: BC 0.812 (K=1,M=0), RANK 0.934 (K=5000,M=0), ground-truth simulator reference 0.952.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Table II, all rows/columns and caption; PDF p. 6, Section V-B, Planning performance
evidence.detail: Rows Push-T/Triangle/Stacking/Swapping: Diffusion Policy 0.642/0.724/0.912/0.680; V-GPS 0.620/0.593/0.972/0.650; LaDi-WM 0.683/0.680/0.933/0.410; DreamerV3 0.649/0.732/0.983/0.700; GPC 0.739/0.767/0.989/0.730. Parenthesized VLM scores are 0.761 and 0.973. Text specifies 50 seeds, common data and pretrained policy, 100 candidates for comparisons; caption distinguishes learned-reward K=100 from VLM K=10. Other task score formulas are not stated.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section V-B, Reward paragraph
evidence.detail: Differentiable ResNet18+MLP reward predictors use numerical objectives such as registration loss or cube distance. Optional ChatGPT-4o selects from final predicted frames at resolution 96 with task-specific prompts, one query per decision and temperature 0.2.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table III, all configuration headers, Score (IoU)/Timing (s) rows and caption
evidence.detail: Over 100 seeds, BC/RANK50/RANK100/OPT25/RANK10+OPT25 score 0.642/0.698/0.739/0.791/0.882, with 0.457/5.835/11.745/39.061/374.102 seconds per decision. The printed BC header says K=1,M=1, unlike Table I's M=0.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Figure 5, legend, bars and score axis; Section V-B, Importance of random exploration
evidence.detail: With-exploration bars exceed without-exploration bars for both RANK and OPT on vision-based Push-T. The axis starts at 0.4; exact bar values, uncertainty and a size-matched data control are not provided. Text describes an approximately 10% improvement without clarifying that percentage convention.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Figures 3–4 and captions; PDF p. 6, Section V-B opening image-quality discussion
evidence.detail: Predicted frames and SSIM assess visual correspondence. Figure 3 uses the full roughly 250-frame evaluation horizon over five seeds; Figure 4 uses ten sampled prediction points and 100 samples per method. These are distinct image-quality protocols, not executed-task success rates.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section V-C, Real-world Vision-based Tasks
evidence.detail: Push-T reward supervision uses AprilTags and registration loss; cloth supervision uses normalized progress from spread clothes through grasp-and-move operations. All inference components use visual observations. Real-world success rates are evaluated over 10 trials.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figure 8, all five bars and Success Rate axis; PDF p. 7, Section V-C trial-count sentence
evidence.detail: Axis-read success rates: Push-T baseline 0.5, RANK 0.7, OPT 0.7; clothes baseline 0.3, RANK 0.7. No error bars, confidence intervals or explicit operational success thresholds are supplied; Section V-C states 10 trials.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figures 6–7 and captions; PDF p. 2, Algorithm 1 instantiation comment
evidence.detail: Real trajectories contrast BC and GPC. Figure 6 labels RANK K=10,M=0 and OPT K=0,M=25; the latter conflicts with Algorithm 1's K=1 OPT warm start. Figure 7 reports cloth RANK K=10,M=0 and no cloth OPT trajectory.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Section VII, Limitation and Future Work
evidence.detail: Authors attribute approximately 90–95% of runtime to diffusion world-model rollouts and report about three seconds per real-world RANK decision. Efficiency improvements are future work.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Appendix A, Tasks and Datasets, complete paragraph and bullets
evidence.detail: Simulation: Push-T 500 expert demos, 6×500 perturbations and seven long-horizon demos; Triangle 30/100, Stacking 50/100, Cube & Sphere 100/100 expert/perturbation trajectories. Real tasks: 100 expert demonstrations per task and five random-play videos of several minutes.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, implementation/training and optimization descriptions; pp. 5–7, evaluation descriptions; p. 8, Appendix A
evidence.detail: These supplied implementation sections give selected policy hyperparameters, world-model horizons and data totals, but omit exact splits, phase schedules, action constraints, optimization step-size values, GPU/software specifications and operational real-world success thresholds.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section III opening notation and implementation paragraph; PDF p. 4, Figure 2 and Two-phase training
evidence.detail: The notation defines a_t:t+T as T+1 actions and inclusive histories, while implementation calls T=16 a prediction horizon and H=2 an observation horizon. Training prose says T applications yield o_t+1:t+T+1, an inclusive T+1-frame range. Exact indexing is unresolved.
